note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: A convex combination of points $\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{k}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ is a linear combination of the form

such that $c_{1} + c_{2} + \cdots + c_{k} = 1$ and $c_{i} \geq 0$ for all $i$. The set of all convex combinations of points in a set $S$ is called the convex hull of $S$, denoted by $\text{conv\,\,\,}S$.﻿

content.paragraph: The convex hull of a single point $\textbf{v}_{1}$ is just the set $\left\{ \textbf{v}_{1} \right\}$, the same as the affine hull. In other cases, the convex hull is properly contained in the affine hull. Recall that the affine hull of distinct points $\textbf{v}_{1}$ and $\textbf{v}_{2}$ is the line
Because the weights in a convex combination are nonnegative, the points in $\text{conv\,\,\,\{}\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2}\text{\}}$ may be written as
which is the line segment between $\textbf{v}_{1}$ and $\textbf{v}_{2}$, hereafter denoted by $\overset{‾}{\textbf{v}_{1}\textbf{v}_{2}}$.﻿

If a set $S$ is affinely independent and if $\textbf{p} \in \text{aff\,\,\,\,\,}S$, then $\mathbf{p} \in \text{conv\,\,\,}S$ if and only if the barycentric coordinates of $\textbf{p}$ are nonnegative. Example 1 shows a special situation in which $S$ is much more than just affinely independent.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: and $S = \left\{ \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\textbf{v}_{3} \right\}$. Note that $S$ is an orthogonal set. Determine whether $\textbf{p}_{1}$ is in $\text{Span~}S$, $\text{aff~}S$, and $\text{conv~}S$. Then do the same for $\textbf{p}_{2}$.﻿
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: If $\textbf{p}_{1}$ is at least a linear combination of the points in $S$, then the weights are easily found, because $S$ is an orthogonal set. Let $W$ be the subspace spanned by $S$. A calculation as in Section 6.3 shows that the orthogonal projection of $\textbf{p}_{1}$ onto $W$ is $\textbf{p}_{1}$ itself:

This shows that $\textbf{p}_{1}$ is in $\text{Span~}S$. Also, since the coefficients sum to $1$, $\textbf{p}_{1}$ is in $\text{aff~}S$. In fact, $\textbf{p}_{1}$ is in $\text{conv~}S,$ because the coefficients are also nonnegative.

For $\mathbf{p}_{2}$, a similar calculation shows that $\text{proj}_{W}\text{\,\,}\mathbf{p}_{2} \neq \mathbf{p}_{2}$. Since $\text{proj}_{W}\text{\,\,}\mathbf{p}_{2}$ is the closest point in $\text{Span~}S$ to $\mathbf{p}_{2}$, the point $\mathbf{p}_{2}$ is not in $\text{Span~}S$. In particular, $\mathbf{p}_{2}$ cannot be in $\text{aff~}S$ or $\text{conv~}S$.﻿

content.paragraph: Recall that a set $S$ is affine if it contains all lines determined by pairs of points in $S$. When attention is restricted to convex combinations, the appropriate condition involves line segments rather than lines.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: A set $S$ is convex if for each $\textbf{p}$, $\textbf{q} \in S$, the line segment $\overline{\mathbf{pq}}$ is contained in $S$.﻿

content.paragraph: Intuitively, a set $S$ is convex if every two points in the set can “see” each other without the line of sight leaving the set. Figure 1 illustrates this idea.

image.alt: Three solids with a line segment inside each of them.

content.paragraph: The next result is analogous to Theorem 2 for affine sets.

note.title: ﻿﻿Theorem ﻿7﻿
note.heading: ﻿﻿Theorem ﻿7﻿
note.paragraph: A set $S$ is convex if and only if every convex combination of points of $S$ lies in $S$. That is, $S$ is convex if and only if $S = \text{conv~}S$.﻿

content.heading: Proof
content.paragraph: The argument is similar to the proof of Theorem 2. The only difference is in the induction step. When taking a convex combination of $k + 1$ points, consider $\textbf{y} = c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1} + \cdots + c_{k}\textbf{v}_{k} + c_{k + 1}\textbf{v}_{k + 1}$, where $c_{1} + \cdots + c_{k + 1} = 1$ and $0 \leq c_{i} \leq 1$ for all $i$. If $c_{k + 1} = 1$, then $\textbf{y} = \textbf{v}_{k + 1}$, which belongs to $S$, and there is nothing further to prove. If $c_{k + 1} < 1$, let $t = c_{1} + \cdots + c_{k}$. Then $t = 1 - c_{k + 1} > 0$ and

By the induction hypothesis, the point $\textbf{z} = (c_{1}/t)\textbf{v}_{1} + \cdots + (c_{k}/t)\textbf{v}_{k}$ is in $S$, since the nonnegative coefficients sum to $1$. Thus equation (1) displays $\textbf{y}$ as a convex combination of two points in $S$. By the principle of induction, every convex combination of such points lies in $S$.﻿

Theorem 9 below provides a more geometric characterization of the convex hull of a set. It requires a preliminary result on intersections of sets. Recall from Section 4.1 (Exercise 40) that the intersection of two subspaces is itself a subspace. In fact, the intersection of any collection of subspaces is itself a subspace. A similar result holds for affine sets and convex sets.

note.title: ﻿﻿Theorem ﻿8﻿
note.heading: ﻿﻿Theorem ﻿8﻿
note.paragraph: Let $\{ S_{\alpha}:\alpha \in A\}$ be any collection of convex sets. Then $\cap_{\alpha \in A}S_{\alpha}$ is convex. If $\{ T_{\beta}:\beta \in B\}$ is any collection of affine sets, then $\cap_{\beta \in B}T_{\beta}$ is affine.

content.heading: Proof
content.paragraph: If $\textbf{p}$ and $\textbf{q}$ are in $\cap S_{\alpha}$, then $\textbf{p}$ and $\textbf{q}$ are in each $S_{\alpha}$. Since each $S_{\alpha}$ is convex, the line segment between $\textbf{p}$ and $\textbf{q}$ is in $S_{\alpha}$ for all $\alpha$ and hence that segment is contained in $\cap S_{\alpha}$. The proof of the affine case is similar.

note.title: Theorem ﻿9﻿
note.heading: Theorem ﻿9﻿
note.paragraph: For any set $S$, the convex hull of $S$ is the intersection of all the convex sets that contain $S$.﻿

content.heading: Proof
content.paragraph: Let $T$ denote the intersection of all the convex sets containing $S$. Since $\text{conv~}S$ is a convex set containing $S$, it follows that $T \subseteq \text{conv~}S$. On the other hand, let $C$ be any convex set containing $S$. Then $C$ contains every convex combination of points of $C$ (Theorem 7), and hence also contains every convex combination of points of the subset $S$. That is, $\text{conv~}S \subseteq C$. Since this is true for every convex set $C$ containing $S$, it is also true for the intersection of them all. That is, $\text{conv~}S \subseteq T.$

Theorem 9 shows that $\text{conv~}S$ is in a natural sense the “smallest” convex set containing $S$. For example, consider a set $S$ that lies inside some large rectangle in $\text{ℝ}^{2}$, and imagine stretching a rubber band around the outside of $S$. As the rubber band contracts around $S$, it outlines the boundary of the convex hull of $S$. Or to use another analogy, the convex hull of $S$ fills in all the holes in the inside of $S$ and fills out all the dents in the boundary of $S$.﻿

content.paragraph: The following theorem is basic in the study of convex sets. It was first proved by Constantin Caratheodory in 1907. If $\textbf{p}$ is in the convex hull of $S$, then, by definition, $\textbf{p}$ must be a convex combination of points of $S$. But the definition makes no stipulation as to how many points of $S$ are required to make the combination. Caratheodory’s remarkable theorem says that in an $n\text{-dimensional}$ space, the number of points of $S$ in the convex combination never has to be more than $n + 1$.﻿

note.title: Theorem 10
note.heading: Theorem 10
note.paragraph: (Caratheodory) If $S$ is a nonempty subset of $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, then every point in $\text{conv~}S$ can be expressed as a convex combination of $n + 1$ or fewer points of $S$.﻿

content.heading: Proof
content.paragraph: Given $\textbf{p}$ in $\text{conv~}S$, one may write $\textbf{p} = c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1} + \cdots + c_{k}\textbf{v}_{k}$, where $\textbf{v}_{i} \in S$, $c_{1} + \cdots + c_{k} = 1$, and $c_{i} \geq 0$, for some $k$ and $i = 1,\ldots,k$. The goal is to show that such an expression exists for $\textbf{p}$ with $k \leq n + 1$.﻿
If $k > n + 1$, then $\{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{k}\}$ is affinely dependent, by Exercise 20 in Section 8.2. Thus there exist scalars $d_{1},\ldots,d_{k}$, not all zero, such that

Since not all of the $d_{i}$ coefficients are zero, we may assume (by reordering subscripts if necessary) that $d_{k} > 0$ and that $c_{k}/d_{k} \leq c_{i}/d_{i}$ for all those $i$ for which $d_{i} > 0$. For $i = 1,\ldots,k$, let $b_{i} = c_{i} - \left( c_{k}/d_{k} \right)d_{i}$. Then $b_{k} = 0$ and
Furthermore, each $b_{i} \geq 0$. Indeed, if $d_{i} \leq 0$, then $b_{i} \geq c_{i} \geq 0$. If $d_{i} > 0$, then $b_{i} =$ $d_{i}\left( c_{i}/d_{i} - c_{k}/d_{k} \right) \geq 0$. By construction,

Thus $\textbf{p}$ is now a convex combination of $k - 1$ of the points $\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{k}$. This process may be repeated until $\textbf{p}$ is expressed as a convex combination of at most $n + 1$ of the points of $S$.﻿

content.paragraph: This result cannot, in general, be improved by decreasing the required number of points. Indeed, given any three non-collinear points in $\text{ℝ}^{2}$, the centroid of the triangle formed by them is in the convex hull of all three, but is not in the convex hull of any two.
